The upcoming tour will also expand on the breadth of King Crimson material they’ll be drawing from. The supergroup was formed by King Crimson alumni Adrian Belew and Tony Levin in early 2024. Steve Vai was recruited to take on the mammoth task of assuming Robert Fripp ’s role. Latest Videos From Guitar World Watch full video here: Since their inception, BEAT have been playing music from the band’s 1980s records with Fripp’s blessing and guidance . But changes are afoot for their next run of shows. Notably, Danny Carey has been replaced by former Frank Zappa and U.K. sticksman Terry Bozio due to the former’s commitments with Tool. Previously, the band’s material had focused on Crimson’s 1980s trio of records, Discipline , Beat , and Three Of A Perfect Pair. Vai had been put through the wringer learning some of Fripp’s most physically demanding parts. They’ve toured across the US, Mexico, South America and Tokyo, and have just completed a tour of 31 European cities. The boss , Fripp, was in attendance in Tallinn, Estonia. BEAT – Frame by Frame (OFFICIAL LIVE VIDEO) - YouTube Watch On This next chapter means that Vai now has some more learning to do, with Thrak’ s more industrial clangor adding a new dimension to their upcoming shows. It also means he gets to share more stages with the “underrated” Belew . His highly specific and exceptionally brilliant guitar technique is studied and revered.” Speaking to Guitar World previously, BEAT’s virtuosic guitar tandem assured fans that they don’t see themselves as the new King Crimson, but they do believe there’s a good degree of legitimacy to their performances. Given that King Crimson remains quiet despite rumors of a new album , they’re filling an important void. Tickets go on sale Friday, August 7 at 10 AM local time. See BEAT for more. Photograph: Francisco Seco/AP View image in fullscreen King Harald V of Norway at the Notre-Dame Cathedral in Luxembourg, after attending at the funeral of the Grand Duke Jean of Luxembourg, May 2019. Photograph: Francisco Seco/AP Norway Obituary King Harald V of Norway obituary Monarch who opened up the Norwegian royal family and its palaces to the public, and married a commoner despite his father’s opposition Stephen Bates Fri 28 Aug 2026 10.07 EDT Last modified on Fri 28 Aug 2026 12.45 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google King Harald V of Norway, who has died aged 89, Europe’s oldest serving monarch, was the country’s third king since it regained independence in 1905 following the dissolution of its union with Sweden. Although he ceased to be head of the Lutheran state church in 2012 and subsequently lost his constitutional status as “holy” six years later, he did exhibit the Scandinavian moderation, stoicism and genial approachability that led a newspaper to name him Norway’s person of the year in 2017. The first Norwegian king to be born in the country since 1370, Harald was also related to both the Swedish and the British royal families. His parents were Crown Prince Olav, who was king as Olav V between 1957 and 1991, and his wife, Princess Märtha, a member of the Swedish royal dynasty. His grandparents were King Haakon VII, the first king of the independent country, who reigned for 52 years from 1905, and his wife, Queen Maud, daughter of Britain’s Edward VII. The family roots are Danish – from the Glücksburg dynasty – as were those of the Duke of Edinburgh and the former Greek royal family. The mixed heritage made him sympathetic to refugees: “It is not easy to say where we come from. Home is where the heart is,” he said. View image in fullscreen King Harald V greets Queen Elizabeth II at the Royal Palace, Oslo, during a state visit, May 2001. Photograph: Fiona Hanson/PA He was Queen Elizabeth II’s second cousin and a knight of the garter. At the time of his birth, Harald was 16th in line to the British throne, though he had fallen in the rankings to around 80th in more recent years. Confusingly, he was not the fifth Harald to rule his country, but the sixth – the 10th-century Harald Bluetooth generally not being assigned a number in the list of Norwegian kings. The king never attracted a picturesque title as did some of his Viking predecessors – such as Bluetooth, Harald Fairhair and Harald Hardrada, who tried to seize the English throne a few weeks before the Norman invasion in 1066 and was killed at the battle of Stamford Bridge. Harald himself was only three at the time of the Nazi invasion of Norway in 1940, and he and his mother and two older sisters, Ragnhild and Astrid, initially fled to Sweden, which, trying to maintain its neutrality while accommodating the Germans’ attack on their neighbour, was reluctant to let them in. It is alleged that the royal party was initially turned back at the border, and allowed to proceed only when the driver of their car threatened to ram it through the border post. Within three months, Harald, his sisters and mother had escaped to the US. They spent the war years in Washington DC and Harald thereafter spoke English with a slight American accent. Meanwhile, Harald’s grandfather and father escaped to England, where they led a government in exile. Famously Haakon, turning up at the BBC to make a broadcast to his people, was asked by a receptionist: “Where did you say you were king of, dear?” Following the liberation of Norway at the end of the war, the family was reunited and Harald was enrolled first at a state primary and then at Oslo cathedral school. From there he studied at Oslo University and the Norwegian military academy, before following in his father’s footsteps to read history, economics and politics at Balliol College, Oxford, where he also rowed for the college. A keen competitive yachtsman, he and his crews represented Norway at successive Olympics in Tokyo in 1964, Mexico City in 1968 and Munich in 1972, and won world championship medals through the 1980s and a European championship gold medal in 2005. If this was a conventional career, much less so was his determination to marry a commoner, Sonja Haraldsen, a shop assistant who was the daughter of an Oslo textile manufacturer, whom he had met at a sailing party in 1959. The friendship was kept secret for several years, partly because of Olav’s reluctance to have the heir to the throne marry someone who was not royal. In the end, Harald forced the issue by declaring to his father that if he was not allowed to marry her he would not marry anyone, thus bringing an end to the dynasty. The couple married in 1968. View image in fullscreen King Harald V aboard the Fram XI vessel, as part of the One Ton Cup international sailing contest, Copenhagen, July 1992. Photograph: Lise Åserud/Reuters Harald was sworn in as king automatically following Olav’s death in January 1991. Although lacking his father’s easy bonhomie, the king attempted successfully – and popularly – to open up the institution and its palace and estates more freely to the public. The Norwegian monarch’s duties are similar to those in Britain, with non-exercised executive power, and all official acts having to be endorsed by the governing council of state, equivalent to a British cabinet. The Norwegian parliament constitutionally debates whether to continue the monarchy every four years, and earlier this year, despite controversies concerning the royal family, voted in favour of its continuation by 141 to 26. The greatest crisis in the country’s modern history occurred on 22 July 2011 when the domestic terrorist Anders Behring Breivik murdered 77 people, mainly at a young socialists’ holiday camp on Utøya island. The king attracted public praise in the wake of the tragedy, when he met bereaved relatives and called for national solidarity and mutual support. He was seen to weep at the memorial service for the victims. Harald was treated for bladder cancer in 2003, contracted Covid, had a pacemaker fitted in 2024 and was being treated for the blood disorder haemolytic anaemia. He is survived by Sonja and their children, Princess Märtha Louise and Prince Haakon, whose wife, Mette-Marit (nee Tjessem-Høiby), was obliged to apologise in February this year for email exchanges with the convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein, in which her name was mentioned nearly 1,000 times. The king said that she had not broken any law. Mette-Marit’s son by a previous relationship, Marius, was jailed for four years in June following convictions for two rapes and drug offences. Haakon succeeds Harald as King Haakon VIII and will adopt the monarchy’s traditional motto: “All for Norway”. "We don't yet have the full picture of this event and we're not able to conduct a full risk assessment," WHO chief Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus said. Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov played down the reports as "false information," insisting only Russian authorities' official statements should be relied on. What has Trump said about the suspected plague situation? Peskov also said he had no information regarding a planned call between US President Donald Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin about the situation, despite Trump announcing such a call was scheduled. Trump said the death of the technician did not appear to be linked to a biological weapon. "We're going to find out soon, but we don't think so," Trump told reporters, adding that Russia claimed the incident was under control. The US did make a formal request for more information on the matter from Russia, the AFP news agency reported. Second suspected case reported This comes after a 28-year-old female technician employed at a plague research institute in the Irkutsk region of Siberia died of the disease, possibly contracting it from a broken test tube. According to the WHO head, Russia should clarify reports of a "second employee with pneumonia of undetermined cause" at the institute. While the United States, the European Union and the WHO have all called on Moscow to be transparent about the case, Russian authorities insist the population in the region is safe. WHO head Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus called for more transparency from Russia Image: World Health Organization/AP Photo/picture alliance "There are no epidemic risks for the population," the country's health agency said, adding its investigations had resulted in "no emergencies" and emphasizing the plague research institute's compliance. "More than 90% of contacts have completed medical observation," the agency added. "The results of almost 5,000 laboratory tests did not reveal any dangerous pathogenic microorganisms." In response to the reports, Mongolia said it implemented "health surveillance and monitoring measures" at the border between the two countries. Pneumonic plague is a highly contagious bacterial infection of the lungs which can pass from person to person through the air, for example, via coughing. Bos , Worthy News Europe Bureau Chief BUDAPEST/KYIV ( Worthy News ) – Diplomatic relations between Hungary and neighboring war-torn Ukraine have again deteriorated, though Budapest called the current standoff a “cold peace, not a cold war.” Tensions increased after revelations that Hungary’s oil and natural gas giant MOL had offered Ukraine’s energy giant Naftogaz storage facilities for Ukrainian fuel. Hungary is a member of the NATO military alliance and was therefore considered less vulnerable to Russian attacks than Ukraine, where Moscow has relentlessly targeted the energy sector. Don’t miss the stories Christians should be watching — subscribe to the Worthy Brief. Additionally, a dispute over Hungary’s role in Ukraine’s Carpathian Eight summit and a related row over minority rights have further strained ties. OIL STORAGE DISPUTE The latest tensions emerged despite efforts by the government of Hungarian Prime Minister Péter Magyar to improve relations with Kyiv after years of hostility under his predecessor, Viktor Orbán. MOL and Naftogaz signed a memorandum on creating strategic fuel reserves for Ukraine, with the Ukrainian company saying the arrangement could provide storage capacity in Hungary close to the Ukrainian border. The proposed facilities were intended to help safeguard Ukrainian fuel supplies from Russian attacks on the country’s energy infrastructure. However, Magyar’s government distanced itself from the project, making clear that it would not support storing strategic Ukrainian fuel reserves in Hungary. CARPATHIAN EIGHT ROW The controversy came as another diplomatic disagreement erupted over the Carpathian Eight, or C8, a Ukrainian-led regional cooperation initiative involving countries in the Carpathian region. Hungary attended the inaugural gathering as an observer but did not sign its declaration, and Budapest subsequently disputed suggestions that it had formally joined the initiative. The disagreement prompted unusually sharp exchanges between officials in Budapest and Kyiv, underscoring how difficult efforts to reset bilateral relations have become. Yet Hungarian officials stressed that dialogue with Ukraine would continue, characterizing the deteriorating relationship as a “cold peace, not a cold war.” MINORITY RIGHTS DISPUTE At the center of the broader dispute remains the situation of ethnic Hungarians in Ukraine’s western Transcarpathia region, which borders Hungary. Budapest has demanded guarantees for the community’s language, cultural and educational rights, arguing that restrictions introduced by Ukraine in recent years weakened rights previously enjoyed by the Hungarian minority. Kyiv says it is addressing Hungarian concerns and insists that Ukraine meets European standards. The dispute has consequences beyond bilateral ties as Hungary has linked further progress in Ukraine’s European Union membership negotiations to resolving the minority-rights questions. EU ACCESSION TALKS As an EU member, Hungary can block key steps in Ukraine’s accession process, and Budapest has withheld approval for opening additional negotiating clusters because of the dispute. The Magyar government has signaled that it supports Ukraine’s entry into the bloc in principle but says Kyiv must first satisfy Hungary’s concerns over the rights of the roughly 100,000-strong Hungarian minority. Hungary’s position toward Ukraine also comes as the country remains heavily dependent on Russian oil and natural gas, complicating Budapest’s efforts to balance relations with Kyiv and Moscow. Additionally, Ukraine has repeatedly targeted Russian energy infrastructure that Kyiv says helps finance Moscow’s invasion, though these actions have also affected deliveries to Hungary. ENERGY INFRASTRUCTURE Russian attacks have also severely damaged Ukraine’s own energy facilities, increasing Kyiv’s need for secure fuel reserves and storage capacity. Despite the bilateral disputes, officials in Hungary and Ukraine have indicated they intend to continue negotiations to prevent a further escalation of diplomatic friction. Yet disagreements over energy cooperation, regional diplomacy and minority rights have complicated attempts by Budapest and Kyiv to establish a more cooperative relationship after years of confrontation.
